lead: A multi-cylinder engine fires its cylinders one after another in a fixed sequence, the firing order, so that the power strokes come at equal intervals and the crankshaft is not hammered from one end. Two related choices decide how the gas gets in and out: the valve layout, which says where the valves sit, and the valve actuation, which says how the cam pushes them open. Together they set how smoothly an engine runs, how well it breathes and how much service it needs.
prereq: You need the four strokes and the 720°CA cycle from four-stroke and two-stroke engines.

blocks.text: The cylinders are numbered from the front (timing-gear or fan end), and cylinder 1 is the reference. In a four-stroke engine each cylinder fires once in 720°CA, so for equal spacing the angle between successive firings, the firing interval, is:

blocks.where: n is the number of cylinders and θ<sub>f</sub> is in crank degrees. A two-stroke cycle lasts 360°, so there θ<sub>f</sub> = 360°/n.

blocks.text: An inline four has θ<sub>f</sub> = 180°. Its crankshaft is flat: throws 1 and 4 point one way and throws 2 and 3 the opposite way, so pistons 1 and 4 reach TDC together, and 180° later pistons 2 and 3 do. Of each pair, one is at the end of compression and fires, while the other is at the end of exhaust.

After cylinder 1 fires, the next TDC belongs to pair 2-3, so either 2 or 3 fires next; then 4 must fire, because 1 has just finished its power stroke and is on exhaust. Only two orders are possible: 1-3-4-2 (the usual one) and 1-2-4-3. The pair 1 and 4 fires in the same order in both; only the pair 2 and 3 changes places. The order 1-2-3-4 is impossible on this crankshaft: the third firing comes at 360°, when only pistons 1 and 4 are at TDC, so it must be cylinder 4.
An inline six (θf = 120°) usually fires 1-5-3-6-2-4, which alternates between the front and rear halves of the engine.

items: Balance and torque: equal intervals give a power pulse every 180° in a four, so the torque on the shaft is steadier and the flywheel can be lighter.
Bearing load: consecutive firings are kept apart along the shaft (1 then 3, not 1 then 2), so neighbouring main bearings are not loaded by two successive power strokes.
Torsional vibration: alternating between the two ends of the shaft reduces the twisting of a long crankshaft.
Breathing: the order decides which exhaust pulses meet in the manifold, and so how well each cylinder empties and fills.

blocks.text: If the spark plug leads or injector pipes are fitted in the wrong order, some cylinders fire at the end of exhaust instead of compression, and the engine runs badly or will not start.
The layout says where the valves sit. Four lettered layouts are named after the shape of the cylinder and chamber in section.

head: Layout
Where the valves sit
Remarks
rows: both in the block, side by side
one low camshaft, cheap; long thin chamber, low compression, poor breathing
one each side of the cylinder, in the block
inlet in the head, exhaust in the block
both in the head above the piston
compact chamber, short flame path, good breathing; all modern engines

blocks.text: The I-head is described further by where its camshaft is: OHV (camshaft in the block, pushrods and rockers), SOHC (one overhead camshaft in the head) and DOHC (two overhead camshafts, one for the inlet valves and one for the exhaust valves). DOHC makes four valves per cylinder easy to drive.

Each valve opens once per cycle, that is once in two crank revolutions, so the camshaft of a four-stroke engine turns at half crank speed: N<sub>cam</sub> = N<sub>crank</sub>/2. It is driven by gears, a roller chain or a toothed belt.

items: A cam lobe lifts a follower (tappet).
In an OHV engine the follower lifts a pushrod, which tilts a rocker arm, which pushes the valve open.
In an OHC engine the lobe presses on a bucket tappet over the valve, or on a finger follower.
A valve spring closes the valve and keeps the follower on the cam.

blocks.text: A small tappet clearance is left in the train so the valve still closes fully when the stem grows with heat; a hydraulic lifter, an oil-filled plunger, takes up that clearance automatically. Pushrods add moving mass, which limits engine speed; overhead camshafts remove them and allow higher speed. A broken timing belt usually lets the pistons strike the open valves.

figure.caption: The inline four’s flat crankshaft puts pistons 1 and 4 at TDC together and 2 and 3 half a turn later. With the order 1-3-4-2 the chart shows which stroke each cylinder is on: in every half-turn exactly one cylinder is on power, as the worked example found for the first one.

spec.aria: Left: side view of a four-throw crankshaft with throws 1 and 4 up and 2 and 3 down. Right: a table of four cylinders by four half-turns. Cylinder 1 runs power, exhaust, intake, compression; cylinder 2 exhaust, intake, compression, power; cylinder 3 compression, power, exhaust, intake; cylinder 4 intake, compression, power, exhaust.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine with firing order 1-3-4-2 runs at 2400 rev/min. Find the firing interval, the time between two firings, and the stroke each cylinder is on during the first half-turn after cylinder 1 fires.
steps: Speed: 2400/60 = 40 rev/s, so 180° (half a turn) takes 0.5/40 = 0.0125 s = 12.5 ms.
Cylinder 1 fires at 0°, 3 at 180°, 4 at 360°, 2 at 540°. Each cylinder runs power, exhaust, intake, compression in turn, 180° each.

From 0° to 180°: cylinder 1 is on power. Cylinder 3 fires at 180°, so it is on compression. Cylinder 4 fires at 360°, so it is one stroke earlier still, on intake. Cylinder 2 fired at 540° of the previous cycle (−180°), so it is on exhaust.
Check: the four cylinders are on four different strokes, as they must be.
examples.answer: θ<sub>f</sub> = 180°, 12.5 ms between firings; in the first half-turn cylinder 1 is on power, 3 on compression, 4 on intake and 2 on exhaust (Figure 1.6.1).

traps: For a four-stroke use 720°/n, not 360°/n; 360°/n is the two-stroke value.
Changing 1-3-4-2 to 1-2-4-3 does not change the firing interval; it only swaps the firing of cylinders 2 and 3.
Do not offer 1-2-3-4 for an inline four: it cannot work on a flat four-throw crankshaft.
L-head means both valves in the block; I-head means both in the head; F-head has one in each; T-head one on each side.
The half-speed camshaft rule is for four-strokes only; a two-stroke camshaft, where fitted, turns at crank speed.

quiz.q: Define firing order and firing interval.
quiz.a: Firing order is the sequence in which the cylinders deliver their power strokes, such as 1-3-4-2. Firing interval is the crank angle between two successive firings, 720°/n in a four-stroke.

quiz.q: What is a hydraulic lifter for?
quiz.a: It takes up the valve clearance automatically with oil pressure, so the train runs quietly and needs no tappet adjustment.

quiz.q: Why is the firing interval of a four-stroke engine 720°/n and not 360°/n?
quiz.a: Each cylinder fires once per cycle and a four-stroke cycle is 720°CA, so n equal firings divide 720°. 360°/n is the two-stroke value.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the L-head layout.
quiz.a: Advantage: one low camshaft drives both valves directly, so it is cheap and compact. Disadvantage: the chamber stretches over the valves, so the flame path is long, compression is low and breathing poor.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder four-stroke runs at 3000 rev/min. Find the firing interval and the time between firings.
quiz.a: θ<sub>f</sub> = 720/6 = 120°. 3000/60 = 50 rev/s, and 120° is one third of a turn: t = (1/3)/50 = 6.67 ms.

quiz.q: A four-stroke runs at 2400 rev/min. Find the camshaft speed and how often one valve opens per minute.
quiz.a: Camshaft 1200 rev/min; each valve opens once per camshaft revolution, 1200 times a minute.

quiz.q: Engines with orders 1-3-4-2 and 1-2-4-3 both fire every 180°. What actually differs?
quiz.a: Only cylinders 2 and 3 swap places; 1 and 4 still fire 360° apart in both. The swap changes which neighbouring cylinders fire one after another, so the loads on the middle main bearings, the twisting of the shaft and the sequence of exhaust pulses in the manifold differ.

quiz.q: Why does a four-valve engine almost always use DOHC?
quiz.a: The inlet valves and the exhaust valves sit in two rows on opposite sides of the chamber. One camshaft would need long rockers to reach both rows; two camshafts can act directly on each row, with less moving mass, and allow inlet and exhaust timing to be shifted separately.

beyond: Cam phasers, switchable cam profiles and cylinder deactivation are now common on passenger cars; electro-hydraulic and camless valve trains are in development. Racing engines use desmodromic or pneumatic valve return for very high speeds. Search for cam phaser, cylinder deactivation and camless engine.
